title: Canadian views of America, taxes and health care
summary: He talks politics and describes Canadian health coverage and Covid subsidies.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Well we’ve been at this for almost an hour, and I appreciate your stories and your career. I wanted to just go off music before we end. I’m wondering what the feeling in Canada has been about America in the last number of years.

I’m just so disappointed. I’m kind of hopeful that this new party, the Democratic party will come in and kind of do something. I’m hoping they’re getting blocked. I’m wishing today that both of those senators become democrats because there could be a whole new change for the country. I mean I’ve always voted Democratic. There’s a couple of times when I maybe thought differently, but most of my ways have been Democratic. But I mean what these guys are pulling now is just really upsetting. I just can’t understand it. And you know I mean I don’t understand, first of all, living in Canada, right, I’ve lived in Canada now since 1974. Born in America. So I remember when I was a kid the word “socialism” was just like oh my God, it’s like you’re going to be you know like socialist, like communists. Socialism is communism. And yet they have social security, and every time a big corporation like the auto industry or anything goes bust socialism kicks in. So these guys are all afraid of it. But in Canada we have basically that kind of system. And

when I first moved here I was really upset about the fact that my taxes all of a sudden, whoa, why am I paying this amount of taxes. I never had to pay a doctor’s bill, two kids born, I mean the medical thing. And you feel so comfortable. There’s that pressure of having the fact that when I was traveling with Buddy every month I had to pay $500 to Blue Cross. If I didn’t get that in — my mother would say make sure your Blue Cross is — you know because if you ever get — you know that fear that you’re going to lose everything if you have to go into the hospital. It’s just not here. And so that’s a big strain off. Now also the other thing is during this period here with Covid, the young musicians who have made $5000 last year, the government gives you $2000 a month subsidy to exist. So every young musician gets $2000. Or anybody that’s out of work who can prove that they made $5000 in the previous year, they’re giving $2000 a month so you can live on. Now it’s just gone down to $1800 because they started taking taxes on it. So young kids who work part time jobs and were earning that kind of money, they get the subsidy basically, from the government. It’s a social system, we may end up paying for it. But just having that — I guess you can’t call it free medical because it’s medical that you pay for, but just having that off your back is a big big weight off your shoulders. And you have this feeling of comfort. I mean I just dislocated my shoulder two weeks ago so I’m working with this shoulder. I had a slip and fall out on a walk. I went out and it was just so painful. I went down and I went right into the hospital emergency. They put me out, they pulled it back, right in. Within three hours I was back home with the shoulder in and they started me on physio. I have another month of physio to go but I wish the U.S. could realize that so what, you pay a little bit more in taxes — people that can’t afford it they’ll end up with it. Guys that can afford it then so what, and then everybody’s covered. I’m telling you, I think that would make a lot of things better down there. I feel, I don’t know, you know you have a teaching job you get it. But if you work with certain companies you have a medical plan. But if you get fired or laid off it’s gone, a lot of it.
